Q: Swap out a low-level dependency A:

Swapping dependencies based on a grand parent is typically a hard problem for DI Containers.

DI Containers like Simple Injector and Ninject have explicit support for conditionally or context-based registering dependencies based on the consuming type. Ninject contains a .WhenInjectedInto method for this, where Simple Injector provides a RegisterConditional method. However, where Ninject allows you to look up the parent hierarchy and base the dependency on the grand parent (your use case), the Simple Injector designers (which includes me) decided not to allow allow registrations to look further up than their direct parent, because "making a decision based on the parent’s parent can lead to all sorts of complications and subtle bugs." This especially happens when the intermediate dependency (AddressFormatter in your case) gets a lifestyle other than Transient as it could lead to Torn and Ambiguous Lifestyles.

Although this explanation doesn't solve your issue, it hopefully gives some background information on what issues can arise from grand-parent based conditional registration.

For MS.DI, the built-in DI Container, however, things get worse, because there is not even support for doing context-based injection through its API.

To solve this, there are multiple workarounds.

Workaround 1: Register the graph completely by hand

One such workaround is registering the part of the object graph that requires the conditionality in a hand-wired fashion. In other words, while you register a type using one of the AddXXX methods on the ServiceCollection, you register a delegate in which you new types by hand.

In your case that would look something as follows:

services.AddTransient<CustomerFileController>(sp =>
    new CustomerFileController(
        formatter: new AddressFormatter(
            anonymiser: new NameAnonymiser(
               dataWriter: new FileDataWriter()))));

services.AddTransient<CustomerDatabaseController>(sp =>
    new CustomerDatabaseController(
        formatter: new AddressFormatter(
            anonymiser: new NameAnonymiser(
               dataWriter: new DatabaseDataWriter()))));

Here we register CustomerFileController and CustomerDatabaseController because that is where the conditionality starts. Accidentally those are also root types (i.e. nothing depends on them), but generally speaking, this doesn't have to be this way.

This method, however, gets pretty tedious and maintenance heavy, because as the object graph changes, so does this registration. For instance, add a dependency to AddressFormatter and you'll have to change both registrations. Further more, when dependencies need different lifestyles, it becomes even more complicated.

A better workaround would, therefore, be a mix between manual registration and auto-wiring.

Workaround 2: Mix auto-wiring with hand-wiring the object graph

This method depends on a less known helper class that ships with MS.DI, named ActivatorUtilities. A solution might look as follows:

container.AddSingleton<FileDataWriter>();
container.AddSingleton<DatabaseDataWriter>();

services.AddTransient<CustomerFileController>(() =>
    ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance<CustomerFileController>(sp,
        ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance<AddressFormatter>(sp,
            ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance<NameAnonymiser>(sp,
                sp.GetRequiredService<FileDataWriter>()))));

services.AddTransient<CustomerDatabaseController>(() =>
    ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance<CustomerFileController>(sp,
        ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance<AddressFormatter>(sp,
            ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance<NameAnonymiser>(sp,
                sp.GetRequiredService<DatabaseDataWriter>()))));

The ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance allows creating new instances of types by pulling in their dependencies from the container, while allowing to override dependencies by passing them in to the method.

Although this code looks convoluted, from maintainability, this is much better, because even when changes to constructors are made, this code keeps working as is.

Still, there are some caveats here, as CreateInstance will always create a new instance, effectively making the created instances transient.

Another issue with ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance is that it circumvents the containers cyclic dependency detection. Where MS.DI will (typically) warn you when you registered a cyclic dependency graph, this detection easily goes out the way whenever you start using ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance in the registration process, which will result in stack-overflow exceptions instead. I learned this the hard way and this has costed me many hours already.

There are many other workarounds, such as making use of keyed registration i.c.w. attributes and also sub typing. But I consider those less practical for your particular case, which is why I leave them out of my answer.

Q: PHP 8.4 OPcache calling wrong internal functions — round() becomes sin(), file_get_contents() becomes unlink() A:

Is it happening on the server ? do you have the same ENV setup on local too ? and does it generate the same error on local when op cache is enabled on local environment? it can be OP cache or it can be memory corruption too. can you confirm that this issue is replicable on local too with the same env.

try memtest86 to validate the memory corruption, another thing is that you mentioned NTS , NTS with FPM is not something that isnt recommended but if extensions mismatched or stale binaries loaded that can also cause this issue .

Q: How to export a MySQL database to JSON? A:

Using MySQL Shell from the MySQL team, you can output directly to JSON in the terminal:

mysqlsh --sql --result-format=json/array --uri=[username]@localhost/[schema_name] --execute "Your SQL query"

You can also output each row as a separate JSON object, (instead of combining all rows into one big JSON array), by passing json instead of json/array, like this:

mysqlsh --sql --result-format=json --uri=exampleuser@localhost/example_schema --execute 'SELECT * FROM example_table'
